### 7.2 The soft photon mode $N_{A}$

Let us finally explore the connection between what we have called the “soft charge” $Q_{\lambda}$ and actual long wavelength soft radiation. At $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , the soft-part of the soft charge is

$$ \displaystyle Q_{\lambda}^{+,S} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}F_{uA}D^{A}\lambda $$

Notice that the only term in the integrand which actually depends on $u$ is $F_{uA}$ . Therefore, if we define the “soft photon mode” $N_{A}$ as

$$ N_{A}\equiv\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\hat{n}}}duF_{uA} $$

which is an integral over $u$ at a fixed angle, we can re-express $Q_{\lambda}^{+,S}$ as the 2-sphere integral

$$ \displaystyle Q_{\lambda}^{+,S}=\int_{S^{2}}d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}N_{A}D^{A}\lambda. $$

Now, why did we name $N_{A}$ the “soft photon mode,” exactly? It’s because it’s a measure of how many soft photons hit $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ per angle over its entire history! Recall that in Lorenz gauge, solutions to the vacuum equations of motion can be Fourier decomposed into linear combinations of plane waves of the form

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu} \displaystyle=\varepsilon_{\mu}e^{-ikx} \displaystyle F_{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=-i(k_{\mu}\varepsilon_{\nu}-k_{\nu}\varepsilon_{\mu})e^{-ikx} $$

where $\varepsilon_{\mu}$ is a polarization vector. $F_{uA}$ in particular is

$$ F_{uA}=-i(\partial_{A}\hat{n}\cdot\vec{\varepsilon})\,k_{0}\,e^{-ikx} $$

where $\vec{\varepsilon}$ is the spatial component of $\varepsilon_{\mu}$ .

In section 5.1, we argued that plane waves on $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ can be expressed (in a distributional sense) as

$$ \evaluated{e^{-ikx}}_{\mathcal{I}^+}=\begin{cases}e^{-ik_{0}u}&\text{ if }\hat{n}=\hat{k}\\
0&\text{ for any other angle}\end{cases}. $$

Therefore, we can measure the amount of radiation which hits $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ at an angle $\hat{n}$ , frequency $\omega$ , polarization vector $\vec{\varepsilon}=\partial_{A}\hat{n}$ as

$$ \begin{matrix}\text{``amount'' of radiation emitted}\\
\text{in the $\hat{n}$-direction with}\\
\text{frequency $\omega$ polarized along $\partial_{A}$}\end{matrix}=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\hat{n}}}du\;e^{i\omega u}F_{uA}. $$

$N_{A}$ is just the $\omega\to 0$ limit of the above expression, confirming that it does indeed measure the “amount” of soft radiation emitted per angle!

One might wonder “where” exactly soft photons are located in the spacetime. Note that if one wants to find the Fourier components of $A_{\mu}$ , one must compute the Fourier transform of $A_{\mu}$ which is an integral over the full 4-dimensional spacetime. This is a highly “non-local” computation, depending on the full history of $A_{\mu}$ . So, while $A_{\mu}$ itself evolves in a manifestly local way, the designation of how many “photons” have been emitted in a spacetime is a non-local notion. What’s more, infinite wavelength soft photons are the most non-local of all. So, while $F_{uA}$ itself is only non-zero at large $r$ when the news that a particle has accelerated finally reaches $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , a soft-photon should be understood as being de-localized over all of null infinity.

*Figure 23: A plane wave hitting future null infinity. The shade of gray represents the phase of the wave. A soft photon can be pictured by taking the infinite wavelength limit.*

In particular, it is possible for accelerating charged particles to both create and destroy soft photons. For instance, if a charge starts travelling at velocity $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ , then accelerates to $\vec{\beta}_{2}$ , and then accelerates back to its original velocity $\vec{\beta}_{1}$ , no net soft photons will have been produced despite the fact that radiation will have been released during both acceleration events.

Because we know that the amount of soft radiation released only depends on the initial and final velocities of the charged particles, we might expect that $N_{A}$ can be expressed in terms of of quantities at $\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\pm}$ . This is indeed the case. Recalling the definitions of $\phi_{+}$ and $\phi_{-}$

$$ \evaluated{A_A}_{\mathcal{I}^+_+}=\partial_{A}\phi_{+},\hskip 14.22636pt\evaluated{A_A}_{\mathcal{I}^+_-}=\partial_{A}\phi_{-} $$

we can see that

$$ \displaystyle N_{A} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\hat{n}}}duF_{uA}=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\hat{n}}}du(\partial_{u}\underbrace{A_{A}}_{O(1)}-\partial_{A}\underbrace{A_{u}}_{O(1/r)}) \displaystyle=A_{A}^{(0)}(u=\infty)-A_{A}^{(0)}(u=-\infty) \displaystyle=\partial_{A}(\phi_{+}-\phi_{-}) \displaystyle=\partial_{A}N $$

where

$$ N\equiv\phi_{+}-\phi_{-}. $$

Amazingly we have found that $N_{A}$ is the total derivative of a single function $N$ which is equal to the difference in the large gauge vacuum modes between early and late times!

Interestingly, $Q_{\lambda}^{+}$ , which a priori is an integral over a 3-dimensional Cauchy surface $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , only truly depends on quantities defined at $\mathcal{I}^{+}_{\pm}$ . This can be seen as an manifestation of Noether’s 1.5th theorem.

### 7.3 Poisson bracket algebra at null infinity

Let us compute the algebra of Poisson brackets of our phase space at null infinity. The symplectic form becomes, using (6.38),

$$ \displaystyle\omega \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}d\Sigma_{\mu}\omega^{\mu}=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}\omega_{u} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\gamma^{AB}(\delta F_{uA}\wedge\delta A_{B}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\gamma^{AB}\big(\delta(\partial_{u}A_{A}^{(0)})\wedge\delta A_{B}^{(0)}\big) $$

One may be concerned that we have excluded timelike infinity from our surface of integration. However, at $i^{+}$ the field is Coulombic and completely specified by locations of the charged particles via the equations of motion. Therefore, the on-shell variations $\delta A_{\mu}$ are 0 at timelike infinity and do not contribute to the symplectic form. The only true degrees of freedom of the electromagnetic field are the radiative ones which hit $\mathcal{I}$ .1212 12 In Lorenz gauge, the e.o.m. becomes $\partial^{2}A^{\mu}=j^{\mu}$ which is an inhomogeneous linear differential equation. One can always add a solution to the homogeneous vacuum equation to $A_{\mu}$ which represents adding pure plane-wave radiation to the spacetime. In particular, the only possible on-shell variations $\delta A_{\mu}$ are radiative.

Amazingly, at null infinity the symplectic structure only depends on $A_{A}^{(0)}$ and its $u$ -derivative. In order to clarify what role $N_{A}$ plays in the symplectic structure, let us separate $A_{A}^{(0)}$ into a “large gauge” $u$ -independent piece and a $u$ -dependent piece $\hat{A}_{A}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\phi\equiv\frac{1}{2}(\phi_{+}+\phi_{-}),\hskip 42.67912ptA^{(0)}_{A}(u,z)=\hat{A}_{A}(u,z)+\partial_{A}\phi(z). $$

Plugging the above expression for $A^{(0)}_{A}$ into (7.18), we arrive at our final expression of

$$ \omega=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\gamma^{AB}\delta(\partial_{u}\hat{A}_{A})\wedge\delta\hat{A}_{B}+\int_{S^{2}}d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\gamma^{AB}\delta N_{A}\wedge\delta(\partial_{B}\phi) $$

Apparently, $\phi$ is the symplectic partner of the soft photon mode $N_{A}$ .

We can now find the Poisson brackets by inverting the symplectic form (7.20) and using (6.25). To begin, $\hat{A}_{A}$ has the Poisson brackets of

$$ \displaystyle\Big\{\partial_{u}\hat{A}_{A}(u_{1},z_{1}),\hat{A}_{B}(u_{2},z_{2})\Big\} \displaystyle=-\frac{\gamma_{AB}}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})\,\delta(u_{1}-u_{2}) \displaystyle\Big\{\hat{A}_{A}(u_{1},z_{1}),\hat{A}_{B}(u_{2},z_{2})\Big\} \displaystyle=-\frac{\gamma_{AB}}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})\,\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{sign}(u_{1}-u_{2}). $$

To get the second line, we integrated the first line with respect to $u$ and found the constant of integration using the fact that Poisson brackets must be anti-symmetric.

The Poisson bracket of $N_{A}$ and $\partial_{B}\phi$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\Big\{N_{A}(z_{1}),\partial_{B}\phi(z_{2})\Big\} \displaystyle=-\frac{\gamma_{AB}}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2}) $$

and the following Poisson brackets vanish:

$$ \displaystyle\Big\{\partial_{u}\hat{A}_{A}(u_{1},z_{1}),N_{B}(z_{2})\Big\} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\Big\{\partial_{u}\hat{A}_{A}(u_{1},z_{1}),\partial_{B}\phi(z_{2})\Big\} \displaystyle=0. $$

The soft charge is equal to

$$ \displaystyle Q^{+}_{\lambda} \displaystyle=Q^{+,H}_{\lambda}+\int_{S^{2}}d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}N_{A}D^{A}\lambda^{+}. $$

The hard part of the soft charge only depends on the background charge current so its Poisson brackets with EM field variables is zero.

$$ \Big\{Q_{\lambda}^{+,H},\hat{A}_{A}(u,z)\Big\}=\Big\{Q_{\lambda}^{+,H},N_{A}(z)\Big\}=\Big\{Q_{\lambda}^{+,H},\partial_{A}\phi(z)\Big\}=0. $$

Therefore, we can immediately see that

$$ \Big\{Q_{\lambda}^{+},A_{A}^{(0)}(u,z)\Big\}=\Big\{Q_{\lambda}^{+},\partial_{A}\phi(z)\Big\}=-\partial_{A}\lambda^{+}(z) $$

and the soft charge generates large gauge transformations exactly as one would hope! Keep in mind that this large gauge transformation acts on the entire spacetime solution of $A_{\mu}$ as a whole.

As a brief aside, it is interesting to note that the soft charge is only constructed out of $N_{A}$ which itself only depends on the difference $\phi_{+}-\phi_{-}$ . Meanwhile, the goldstone mode $\phi$ only depends on the sum $\phi_{+}+\phi_{-}$ . If we use the intuition presented in Figure 14, we can see why this is natural. A large $u$ -independent gauge transformation preserves the difference of $\phi_{+}$ and $\phi_{-}$ while changing the sum. Therefore, if we flow along the Hamiltonian vector field $X_{Q_{\lambda}}$ , the difference $\phi_{+}-\phi_{-}$ will remain constant along the flow while the sum $\phi_{+}+\phi_{-}$ will not.

While the hard part $Q^{+,H}_{\lambda}$ did not play a role in the Poisson algebra of our EM field, it would play a role if our charge current $j^{\mu}$ was the global $U(1)$ Noether current of a dynamical matter field $\psi$ with Poisson bracket

$$ \Big\{j^{0}(t,\vec{x}),\psi(t,\vec{y})\Big\}=ie\delta^{3}(\vec{x}-\vec{y})\psi(t,\vec{y}). $$

The hard part would therefore act on $\psi(x)$ as

$$ \Big\{Q^{H}_{\lambda},\psi(x)\Big\}=ie\lambda(x)\psi(x). $$

This means that $Q^{+,H}_{\lambda}$ generates the action of large gauge transformations on the matter field just as $Q^{+,S}_{\lambda}$ generates the action of large gauge transformations on the EM field.

What about the Poisson bracket of $N$ and $\phi$ , namely $\{N,\phi\}$ ? To find it, we can plug $N_{A}=\partial_{A}N$ into the symplectic form (7.20), integrate by parts and read off

$$ D^{2}\Big\{N(z_{1}),\phi(z_{2})\Big\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2}). $$

Solving this equation would give us $\{N,\phi\}$ . The only issue is that this equation cannot actually be solved. This can be seen by integrating $z_{1}$ over the 2-sphere and using the divergence theorem—the LHS will be 0 but the RHS will be 1. Having said that, the modified equation

$$ D^{2}G_{S^{2}}(z_{1}-z_{2})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})-\frac{1}{4\pi} $$

can be solved, and its solution is

$$ G_{S^{2}}(z_{1}-z_{2})=\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\big(|\hat n(z_1) - \hat n(z_2) |^2\big). $$

So what is going on? What is $\{N,\phi\}$ ?

The resolution involves the fact that $\phi$ is really only defined up to a constant, so $\phi\sim\phi+c$ . Therefore, the value of $\phi$ at a point $z$ is not actually a valid function on the phase space. However, the difference of $\phi$ at two different points, is. This would imply

$$ \Big\{N(z_{1}),\phi(z_{2})-\phi(z_{3})\Big\}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\big(|\hat n(z_1) - \hat n(z_2)|^2\big)-\frac{1}{4\pi}\log\big(|\hat n(z_1) - \hat n(z_3)|^2\big) $$

resolving the apparent paradox. We can see that the derivative of $\phi$ has a well-defined Poisson brackets because it is a limit of differences of $\phi$ at two points.

Anyway, aside from this thorny issue of addition by a constant, one may get the feeling that the phase space of electromagnetism is a little too simple. The complete phase space is given by only four functions (and two of them don’t even depend on $u$ !)

$$ \begin{split}(\text{Cauchy data on }\mathcal{I}^{+})=\big(\hat{A}_{A}(u,z),N(z),\phi(z)\big).\end{split} $$

However, actually finding the full solution to the equations of motion based on this Cauchy data is a non-trivial task. Therefore, all the complication resides in the map

$$ \begin{split}(\text{Cauchy data on }\mathcal{I}^{-})\longrightarrow(\text{Cauchy data on }\mathcal{I}^{+})\end{split} $$

which depends on the exact knowledge of the locations of the charged particles in the bulk at all times.

To conclude this section, let me point out that we were able to invert the symplectic form and solve for the Poisson brackets without ever choosing a gauge slice. Shouldn’t this have been impossible, because without doing so the symplectic form isn’t be invertible? Interestingly, this issue was avoided because we pushed our Cauchy slice to $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ where trivial gauge symmetries do not act and the symplectic form really is invertible.

## 8 Electromagnetic Memory

We will now describe a thought experiment, developed in [16, 17], which can detect large gauge vacuum transitions. The basic measurement device, depicted in Figure 24, is a test charge immersed in a tank of viscous fluid.

*Figure 24: A test charge in a tank of viscous fluid.*

Imagine this fluid supplies a linear damping force (i.e. Stokes’ drag) such that the equation of motion for the position of the particle is

$$ m\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\vec{x}=\vec{F}_{\rm ext}-b\frac{d}{dt}\vec{x} $$

where $\vec{F}_{\rm ext}$ is the external force on the particle and $b$ is a proportionality constant which sets the strength of the damping force. Integrating both sides of (8.1), we get

$$ m\Delta\vec{v}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\vec{F}_{\rm ext}-b\Delta\vec{x}. $$

Assume our particle starts at rest and $\vec{F}_{\rm ext}$ is only non-zero for some finite length of time. Then as long as $b>0$ , the particle will eventually come to rest once again. This implies that $\Delta\vec{v}=0$ and

$$ \Delta\vec{x}=\frac{1}{b}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\vec{F}_{\rm ext}. $$

Therefore, the final displacement of the particle in the tank only depends on the time integral of the external force and $b$ .

Now, imagine arranging a large number of these paritcle-in-a-vat apparatuses in a very big sphere which surrounds some charged bulk particles which are scattering/accelerating/radiating. If we assume our test charges move slowly then they’ll only feel a force from the electric field and not the magnetic field. If we write the tangential component of the tiny displacement vector $\Delta\vec{x}$ in spherical coordinates, we find

$$ \displaystyle\Delta x_{A} \displaystyle=\frac{e}{b}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}duF_{uA} \displaystyle=\frac{e}{b}\Delta A_{A}^{(0)} \displaystyle=\frac{e}{b}N_{A} $$

Thus we see that the change in the tangential position of the test charge is proportional to the soft photon mode $N_{A}$ ! Note that because $\Delta x_{A}=r\partial_{A}\hat{n}\cdot\Delta\vec{x}$ , the overall displacement shrinks as $1/r$ .

It should be emphasized that the fact that the test particles have some overall displacement is not particularly interesting. What is interesting is that these displacements depend only on the initial and final velocities of the bulk particles, which is because that is all $N_{A}$ depends on. Hence the name “memory.”

## 9 Is this holography? What information does $Q_{\lambda}$ hold?

Noether’s 1.5th theorem implies that gauge theories have intrinsically holographic properties. Because the Noether current of a gauge symmetry satisfies

$$ J^{\mu}_{\lambda}=\partial_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{\lambda} $$

the soft charge $Q_{\lambda}$ is really a surface charge. Can we somehow use this fact to construct a dual “boundary theory” to electromagnetism?

Nobody knows the answer to this question, but its certainly worth speculating on. One of the first distinctions we must make is between “trivial” holography and true holography. By pushing a Cauchy surface up to $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , can we automatically say that we have collected all of the information of the system onto a spacetime of one fewer dimension? Not really. A true holographic principle would be more like AdS/CFT, where each spatial slice in the bulk corresponds to a spatial slice in the boundary. In our case, while points on $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ with different values of $u$ really just live on a single Cauchy slice, it is also not unnatural to consider $u$ as a time coordinate under which a 2D celestial sphere “evolves.”

*Figure 25: A large holographic cylinder surrounding a scattering event. Imagine a boundary observer had access to $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ measured at each sphere of constant $u$ .*

Let’s see if we can ascertain exactly what bulk information $Q_{\lambda}$ does and does not have access to, in hopes of assessing the possibility of “bulk reconstruction.” Consider the set up drawn in Figure 25. We have a collection of charged particles scattering in the bulk which are confined to be in a sphere of radius $r_{s}$ . Far away from these particles we have another large sphere of radius $r$ , with $r\gg r_{s}$ . Imagine we have access to the soft charges $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ , as measured on the sphere of constant $u$ , for all $\lambda$ and $u$ . When the particles in the bulk radiate, soft charge will flow out of the cylinder and $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ will change with time.

If one knows $Q_{\lambda}$ for all $\lambda$ , one knows the leading $1/r^{2}$ component of the radial electric field $E_{r}$ at all angles. If the particle is travelling at a constant velocity this will only depend on the velocity of the particle. Specifically, in the $u$ fixed large $r$ limit,

$$ E_{r}=\frac{e}{4\pi r^{2}}\frac{1-\beta^{2}}{(1-\vec{\beta}\cdot\hat{n})}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{r_{s}}{r}\right). $$

So, at first glance it seems as though $Q_{\lambda}$ only only holds information about the velocity of charges particles but not the positions of charged particles. The positions of the particles only affect $Q_{\lambda}$ at sub-leading order in $1/r$ .

However, if we truly know $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ for all $u$ , this conclusion is too hasty. Consider the scenario in Figure 26. A charged particle accelerates when it is at a distance of $d$ from the origin. The news of this event will not reach all points of the boundary at the same moment in time. If the point on the boundary closest to the particle gets the news at $u$ , then the antipodal point will get the news at $u+2d$ . Therefore, if one can cross-correlate $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ measurements at different times, one should be able to extract detailed information about the positions of the charged particles when they undergo scattering.

*Figure 26: A charged particle accelerates at a distance of $d$ from the origin. News of this event first reaches the large cylinder at one particular angle at $u$ . However, news of the event reaches the antipodal angle at $u+2d$ .*

In fact, if one knows $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ for all $u$ , one is essentially measuring the soft flux which leaves the sphere at all times. This is tantamount to knowing $F_{uA}=\partial_{u}A_{A}$ for all angles and $u$ . Therefore, knowledge of $Q_{\lambda}(u)$ allows one to reconstruct $A_{A}^{(0)}$ (up to a large gauge transformation) which is essentially all of the Cauchy data at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ by (7.35). If we assume that no radiation enters from $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ , then knowledge of the radiative Cauchy data at both $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ is enough to allow us reconstruct the precise path of the particle in the bulk. In fact, it’s not even particularly hard. From (4.27), essentially reproduced below,

$$ A^{(0)}_{A}=-\frac{e}{4\pi}\frac{\partial_{A}\hat{n}\cdot\vec{\beta}}{1-\vec{\beta}\cdot\hat{n}}+\partial_{A}\Phi_{\rm arbitrary} $$

we can see how $\vec{\beta}$ can be read off of $A^{(0)}_{A}$ , up to a large gauge transformation. The presence of the arbitrary gauge piece does not invalidate the overall procedure because it is $u$ -independent, meaning that if the particle accelerates then one can extract $\vec{\beta}_{i}$ and $\vec{\beta}_{f}$ using the difference $\Delta A_{A}^{(0)}$ . What’s more, one is always able to find $\vec{\beta}_{i}$ using an initial soft charge measurement.

If we have multiple particles in the bulk instead of just one, the situation complicates. Soft charges cannot distinguish between one particle of charge $2e$ and two particles of charge $e$ if they have equal velocities. Having said that, if one keeps track of the positions of the individual particles using the timing method discussed previously, the two particles will generically be able to be resolved.

Therefore, the prospects of bulk reconstruction in classical electromagnetism are actually very promising: almost all of the information about the path of the particle ends up imprinted on $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ . But, at the end of the day, one has to wonder if this really amounts to ‘true’ holography or if this is just ‘trivial’ holography with extra steps. In particular, is the bulk theory equivalent to a boundary theory which has its own intrinsic and non-trivial mathematical formulation? Who knows!

If one graduates from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics, the ability to perform this thought experiment and execute bulk reconstruction encounters major complications, as discussed originally in [47]. If one really wanted to measure $E_{r}$ at large $r$ , because $E_{r}\sim 1/r^{2}$ this measurement would have to be extremely sensitive. However, quantum field fluctuations would preclude one from accurately measuring $\langle E_{r}\rangle$ in some small region of space without waiting a very long time. In fact, the period of time one would have to wait to measure $\langle E_{r}\rangle$ with any accuracy will increase without bound as $r$ increases. Quantum fluctuations make it impossible to measure asymptotic charges in a finite length of time.

Having said that, statistical uncertainty which precludes the efficient measurement of quantum systems is not usually considered to be an essential obstacle in the formulation of theories. (For instance, the black hole information paradox is usually formulated without considering whether it is statistically feasible to determine if Hawking radiation is truly unitary.) The seeming ease with which the bulk can be reconstructed classically could be interpreted as an encouraging sign that it may indeed be possible.

## Appendix A Covariant Integration

### A.1 Helpful formulae

We begin with the handy identity

$$ \delta\sqrt{-g}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\nu}\delta g_{\mu\nu}. $$

Using the fact that $g^{\alpha\beta}$ is symmetric, we can see that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\partial_{\nu}\sqrt{-g} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\nu}g_{\alpha\beta} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}g^{\alpha\beta}(\partial_{\nu}g_{\alpha\beta}+\partial_{\beta}g_{\alpha\nu}-\partial_{\alpha}g_{\beta\nu}) \displaystyle=g^{\alpha\beta}\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\nu} \displaystyle=\Gamma^{\mu}_{\;\mu\nu}. $$

We can use this to derive the indispensable formula

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\mu}J^{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\;\mu\nu}J^{\nu} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\partial_{\mu}(\sqrt{-g}J^{\mu}). $$

This formula allows for one to integrate by parts with $\nabla_{\mu}$ and the covariant measure $\sqrt{-g}d^{4}x$ just as one one would with $\partial_{\mu}$ and $d^{4}x$ in flat space.

We can also derive a similar formula for an anti-symmetric rank-2 tensor $K^{\mu\nu}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\mu}K^{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=\partial_{\mu}K^{\mu\nu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\;\mu\rho}K^{\rho\nu}+\Gamma^{\nu}_{\;\mu\rho}K^{\mu\rho} \displaystyle=\partial_{\mu}K^{\mu\nu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\;\mu\rho}K^{\rho\nu} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}\partial_{\mu}(\sqrt{-g}K^{\mu\nu}). $$

This formula immediately generalizes to anti-symmetric tensors of any rank. It allows one to switch back and forth between equations like $J^{\mu}=\partial_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu}$ and $J^{\mu}=\nabla_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu}$ at the small cost of redefining $J^{\mu}$ and $K^{\mu\nu}$ by factors of $\sqrt{-g}$ .

### A.2 Surface elements and Stokes’ theorem

For a complete treatment of covariant integration see chapter 2 of [48]. Say you have a $3$ -surface $\Sigma$ parameterized by some variables $y^{a}$ . The surface is given by $x^{\mu}=x^{\mu}(y)$ , where $\mu=0,1,2,3$ and $a=1,2,3$ . The tangent space of $\Sigma$ is spanned by the three vectors $e^{\mu}_{a}$ defined by

$$ e^{\mu}_{a}\partial_{\mu}=\partialderivative{x^\mu}{y^a}\partial_{\mu}. $$

You can restrict the metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ to $\Sigma$ to get the induced metric $h_{ab}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2}_{\Sigma} \displaystyle=g_{\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}dx^{\nu} \displaystyle=g_{\mu\nu}\Big(\partialderivative{x^\mu}{y^a}dy^{a}\Big)\Big(\partialderivative{x^\nu}{y^b}dy^{b}\Big) \displaystyle=h_{ab}dy^{a}dy^{b} $$

where we have defined

$$ h_{ab}\equiv g_{\mu\nu}\frac{\partial x^{\mu}}{\partial y^{a}}\frac{\partial x^{\nu}}{\partial y^{b}}=g_{\mu\nu}e^{\mu}_{a}e^{\nu}_{b}. $$

When we want to integrate over this 3-surface, we use the volume measure

$$ d\Sigma\equiv|h|^{1/2}d^{3}y $$

where $h=\det(h_{ab})$ . Let us now introduce the outward-pointing normal vector $n^{\mu}$ which is orthogonal to all $e^{\mu}_{a}$ and has norm $n^{\mu}n_{\mu}=+1(-1)$ if $n^{\mu}$ is timelike (spacelike). We can define the directed surface element

$$ \displaystyle d\Sigma^{\mu} \displaystyle\equiv\pm n^{\mu}d\Sigma \displaystyle d\Sigma_{\mu} \displaystyle=\pm n_{\mu}d\Sigma. $$

where the sign choice of $\pm$ is $+$ $(-)$ if $n^{\mu}$ is timelike (spacelike)1313 13 If you don’t understand the need for the sign, consider that in $(t,r,z^{A})$ coordinates, the outward pointing normal to an $r=const$ surface is given by $n^{\mu}=(0,1,0,0)$ . Upon lowering, we get $n_{\mu}=(0,-1,0,0)$ .. The case when $n^{\mu}$ is null must be handled separately.

We now have the ingredients to covariantly express the divergence theorem. Say $V$ is a 4-volume and $\Sigma=\partial V$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{V}d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}\nabla_{\mu}J^{\mu} \displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu} \displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}d^{3}y\sqrt{|h|}(\pm n_{\mu})J^{\mu}. $$

The above expression can be easily proven if one chooses a coordinate system in which $\Sigma$ is the $x^{0}=1$ surface, $n^{\mu}=(1,0,0,0)$ , and the metric factorizes on $\Sigma$ as

$$ \evaluated{g_{\mu\nu}}_{\Sigma}=\begin{pmatrix}\pm 1&0\\
0&h_{ab}\end{pmatrix}. $$

*Figure 27: Diagram of coordinate system in which the divergence theorem is easy to prove.*

We can define an analogous surface element for a 2-surface $S$ . Say you parametize $S$ by some variables $z^{A}$ . The surface is given by $x^{\mu}=x^{\mu}(z)$ where $A=1,2$ . The induced metric on $S$ is given by

$$ \gamma_{AB}\equiv g_{\mu\nu}\frac{\partial x^{\mu}}{\partial z^{A}}\frac{\partial x^{\nu}}{\partial z^{B}}. $$

We can define the surface element by

$$ dS\equiv\sqrt{\gamma}d^{2}z. $$

Say $n^{\mu}$ and $m^{\mu}$ are two unit vectors which are normal to $S$ . Note that exactly one of $n^{\mu}$ and $m^{\mu}$ will timelike and the other will be spacelike. We define the directed surface element by

$$ dS_{\mu\nu}\equiv-(n_{\mu}m_{\nu}-n_{\mu}m_{\nu})dS. $$

Say $S=\partial\Sigma$ . We can covariantly express Stokes’ theorem as

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Sigma}d\Sigma_{\mu}\nabla_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=\int_{S}d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}(-n_{\mu}m_{\nu})K^{\mu\nu}. $$

Actually, for the above formula to be true, we must choose for $m^{\mu}$ to be outward pointing from $\Sigma$ , as shown in Figure 28.

*Figure 28: $m^{\mu}$ must be defined as the outward pointing normal on $\partial\Sigma$ .*

### A.3 How to integrate over $\mathcal{I}^{+}$

In this note, we frequently use the equation

$$ \int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}J_{u}. $$

The purpose of this section is to derive the above formula, as its proof is a bit subtle. Recall that in $(u,r,z^{A})$ coordinates, the metric is

$$ ds^{2}=du^{2}+2dudr-r^{2}\gamma_{AB}dz^{A}dz^{B}. $$

A point on $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is reached by holding $u$ and $z^{A}$ fixed and sending $r\to\infty$ . Therefore, $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ is defined as the $r=const$ surface where that constant is going to infinity.1414 14 One may be confused because an $r=const$ suface has signature $(1,2)$ while $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ should be a null surface with signature $(0,2)$ . Crucially, $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ should really be understood as a null surface in the conformal compactification where one multiplies the metric by $1/r^{2}$ . The outward pointing normal of this $r=const$ surface in $(u,r,z^{A})$ coordinates is

$$ \displaystyle n^{\mu} \displaystyle=(-1,1,0,0) \displaystyle n_{\mu} \displaystyle=(0,-1,0,0). $$

This implies that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}J^{r} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(J_{u}-J_{r}) $$

which does not quite look like (A.27) due to the presence of $J_{r}$ . We will now argue that for the flux integral of a typical conserved current $J^{\mu}$ , the $J_{r}$ integral will be subleading and vanish as $r\to\infty$ , leaving only the $J_{u}$ part.

We begin by assuming that the total charge $\int d^{3}xJ^{0}$ on a $t=const$ time slice is finite and that a finite amount of flux will pass through $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , which from (A.31) implies

$$ J^{r}\sim\mathcal{O}(1/r^{2}). $$

The current conservation equation then reads

$$ 0=\nabla_{\mu}J^{\mu}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{r^{2}}\partial_{r}(r^{2}J^{r})}_{\mathcal{O}(1/r^{4})}+\partial_{u}J^{u}+\nabla_{A}J^{A}. $$

Using

$$ \displaystyle J^{u} \displaystyle=J_{r} \displaystyle J^{r} \displaystyle=J_{u}-J_{r} $$

we find that

$$ J_{r}=\nabla_{A}(...)^{A}+\mathcal{O}(1/r^{4}) $$

meaning $J_{r}$ is a total derivative on the sphere plus a piece which shrinks as $1/r^{4}$ . Therefore, the integral of $J_{r}$ in (A.32) will go to $0$ as $r\to\infty$ . This proves (A.27).

While we have given a satisfactory proof of (A.27), it is still reassuring to check that the $J_{r}$ piece really is subleading in some key examples. We will now turn to two such examples. One will be where $J^{\mu}$ is the EM Noether’s theorem gauge transformation current $J^{\mu}_{\lambda}$ , and the other will be where $J^{\mu}$ is the charge current $j^{\mu}$ of a massless particle.

#### A.3.1 Example 1: Integrating the Noether current $J^{\mu}_{\lambda}$

The Noether current of gauge symmetry (defined in (3.9)) in EM is

$$ (J_{\lambda})_{\mu}=-F_{\mu\nu}\nabla^{\nu}\lambda+\lambda j_{\mu}. $$

We take the gauge parameter to only depend on the sphere coordinates, so $\lambda=\lambda(z^{A})$ . From the previous section, we want to ensure that the $(J_{\lambda})_{r}$ integral is $0$ , which we now do:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(J_{\lambda})_{r} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(-F_{rA}\nabla^{A}\lambda+\lambda j_{r}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}\,\lambda(\nabla^{A}F_{rA}+j_{r}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}\,\lambda(-\nabla^{u}F_{ru}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}\,\lambda\underbrace{(-\nabla_{r}F_{ru})}_{\mathcal{O}(1/r^{4})} \displaystyle=0. $$

In the first line we integrated by parts on the 2-sphere. In the second line we used the equations of motion $\nabla^{\mu}F_{\mu\nu}=j_{\nu}$ . In the third line we used that $F_{ru}\sim\mathcal{O}(1/r^{2})$ from (4.30). We have now proved that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(J_{\lambda})_{u} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(-F_{uA}\nabla^{A}\lambda+\lambda j_{u}). $$

#### A.3.2 Example 2: Integrating the charge flux of a massless particle

If a massless particle of charge $e$ travels on a path parameterized by affine parameter $\tau$ as

$$ \displaystyle u \displaystyle=u_{0} \displaystyle r \displaystyle=\tau \displaystyle z^{A} \displaystyle=z^{A}_{0} $$

then its charge current will be given by

$$ \displaystyle j^{u} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle j^{r} \displaystyle=\frac{e}{r^{2}}\delta(u-u_{0})\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z^{A}-z^{A}_{0}) \displaystyle j^{A} \displaystyle=0. $$

Note that $j^{u}=0$ because $j^{\mu}$ is the charge flux passing through an $x^{\mu}=const$ surface, and our particle will not pass through any $u=const$ surfaces. In any case,

$$ \displaystyle j_{u} \displaystyle=j^{u}+j^{r}=\frac{e}{r^{2}}\delta(u-u_{0})\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\delta^{2}(z^{A}-z^{A}_{0}) \displaystyle j_{r} \displaystyle=j^{u}=0 $$

and the full flux integral is

$$ \int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}d\Sigma_{\mu}j^{\mu}=\int_{\mathcal{I}^{+}}du\,d^{2}z\sqrt{\gamma}\,r^{2}(j_{u}-j_{r})=e. $$

## Appendix B Noether’s Theorems

For this section we will reintroduce the “weak equality” symbol “ $\approx$ ”. We use weak equality for equations which only hold on solutions to the equations of motion (on-shell), so

$$ \text{e.o.m.}\approx 0. $$

We use strong equality “ $=$ ” for mathematical identities which are always true (off-shell) such as $\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=0$ . Much of the following is based on [15].

### B.1 Noether’s 1st Theorem

Say you have field $\phi_{i}$ and an action

$$ S=\int d^{4}x\,\mathcal{L}. $$

If you have a symmetry transformation

$$ \delta\phi_{i}=\epsilon\delta_{\rm sym}\phi_{i} $$

where $\epsilon$ is an infinitesimal constant, then the action will change by the total derivative of some vector $\mathcal{J}^{\mu}$ .

$$ \delta S=\int d^{4}x\;\epsilon\,\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{J}^{\mu} $$

If we now make $\epsilon$ a spacetime dependent function, i.e. $\epsilon=\epsilon(x)$ , and change the symmetry variation to

$$ \delta\phi_{i}=\epsilon(x)\delta_{\rm sym}\phi_{i} $$

then the variation of the action must be of the form

$$ \delta S=\int d^{4}x\big(\epsilon\,\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{J}^{\mu}+(\partial_{\mu}\epsilon)\mathcal{K}^{\mu}\big). $$

This is because the above equation must reduce to (B.4) when $\epsilon=const$ . In principle, if $S$ depends on higher derivatives of $\phi_{i}$ , there could also be terms which depend on $\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}\epsilon$ , $\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\rho}\epsilon$ , etc., but for brevity we will assume this is not the case. If we take $\epsilon$ to have compact support, we can integrate by parts to find

$$ \delta S=\int d^{4}x\;\epsilon\,\partial_{\mu}\big(\mathcal{J}^{\mu}-\mathcal{K}^{\mu}\big). $$

Finally, recall that a solution to the equations of motion will make the action stationary, and $\delta S\approx 0$ for any variation, including our symmetry variation (B.5). Allowing $\epsilon$ to be any function implies that the current

$$ J_{\mu}\equiv\mathcal{J}^{\mu}-\mathcal{K}^{\mu} $$

is conserved

$$ \partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}\approx 0. $$

This is Noether’s 1st theorem; a symmetry which leaves the action invariant up to a total derivative can be used to find a current which is conserved on-shell.

The proof we have given also provides us an effective method to find these conserved currents. If you have a symmetry variation, simply multiply it by a spacetime dependent infinitesimal parameter $\epsilon(x)$ and deduce the equation which must hold to have $\delta S\approx 0$ on-shell. This equation will be guaranteed to be a conservation equation of the form $\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}\approx 0$ by our proof above.

### B.2 Noether’s 2nd Theorem

Noether’s 2nd theorem states that every gauge symmetry implies there is an off-shell relationship between the equations of motion. In particular, it means that the equations of motion are not all independent. We will define a “gauge symmetry” as an infinite dimensional symmetry which is locally parametized by a spacetime dependent function.

The proof is perhaps easiest to understand using a specific example rather than formulating it in complete generality. Say we have the gauge field $A_{\mu}$ , the external current $j^{\mu}$ , and the action

$$ S=\int d^{4}x\left(-\frac{1}{4}F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}-j^{\nu}A_{\nu}\right). $$

For any variation $\delta A_{\mu}$ , the action will vary as

$$ \displaystyle S \displaystyle=\int d^{4}x\big(-F^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\delta A_{\nu}-j^{\nu}\delta A_{\nu}\big) \displaystyle=\int d^{4}x\big(-\partial_{\mu}(F^{\mu\nu}\delta A_{\nu})+(\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}-j^{\nu})\delta A_{\nu}\big) $$

which yields the equations of motion $E^{\nu}\approx 0$ where

$$ E^{\nu}\equiv\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}-j^{\nu}. $$

This action has a gauge symmetry

$$ \delta A_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\lambda $$

under which $\delta S=0$ off-shell. Therefore, if we choose $\lambda$ to be compact, we have

$$ \displaystyle 0=\delta S \displaystyle=\int d^{4}x\,E^{\nu}\partial_{\nu}\lambda \displaystyle=-\int d^{4}x\,\lambda\partial_{\nu}E^{\nu}. $$

This can only hold for arbitary $\lambda$ if we have the off-shell equation

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\partial_{\nu}E^{\nu} \displaystyle=\partial_{\nu}\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}-\partial_{\nu}j^{\nu}. $$

Therefore, we see that gauge symmetries can be used to find off-shell relationships between the equations of motion, completing our proof of Noether’s 2nd theorem.

Let us reflect briefly on how this proof compares to that of Noether’s 1st theorem. In both proofs, one needs some sort of varying arbitrary function in order get the final result. In Noether’s 1st theorem, it was $\epsilon(x)$ ; in Noether’s 2nd theorem, it was $\lambda(x)$ . The difference is that in Noether’s 1st theorem, the transformation that depended on $\epsilon(x)$ was not really a symmetry of the action (even though it reduced to one when $\epsilon=const$ ) and we only had $\delta S\approx 0$ on-shell, meaning our conservation equation only held on-shell. However, in Noether’s 2nd theorem, we had a gauge symmetry transformation which left $\delta S=0$ off-shell and already depended on an arbitrary function $\lambda(x)$ without the need of $\epsilon(x)$ . Because $\delta S=0$ off-shell, we could find an equation which held off-shell.

Incidentally, Noether’s 2nd theorem should not really come as a surprise. If you have a Lagrangian with a gauge symmetry, you can take a solution to the equations of motion and gauge transform it by a function $\lambda$ whose value and derivatives all vanish on the $t=0$ slice, giving you two solutions to the equations of motion with the exact same initial conditions. This means that the equations of motion cannot be ‘‘predictive,’’ in the sense that initial conditions cannot determine unique solutions.1515 15 By declaring that two solutions are “equivalent” if they differ by a gauge transformation, we restore the predictivity of the equations. This is exactly the behavior which results from the equations of motion not all being independent.

This might make Noether’s 2nd theorem seem trivial and uninteresting. However, that is far from the truth. Let’s take a closer look at (B.18). We see that Noether’s 2nd theorem implies that $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ . This, however, is a strange conclusion, because $j^{\mu}$ is an external current which a priori could be completely arbitrary. What we have seen is that the equations of motion are literally inconsistent unless this external current is constrained to satisfy $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ . This leads us to conclude that fields with gauge symmetries can only couple consistently to currents which are conserved.

This can be seen as a reason why gauge theories are desirable in the first place. If one is trying to concoct a theory in which a field couples to a conserved current, using a field with a gauge symmetry is a great way to accomplish this task!

Noether’s 2nd theorem also illuminates the common procedure where one “promotes” a global symmetry to a gauge symmetry, coupling a matter field to a newly defined gauge field in the process. For instance, the free Dirac field $\psi$ has a global $U(1)$ symmetry $\psi\mapsto e^{-i\theta}\psi$ . If one substitutes $\theta\to\lambda(x)$ , promotes this to a gauge symmetry, and tries to make sure the overall action is invariant under this gauge symmetry, one will find that the Dirac field has coupled to a gauge field $A_{\mu}$ . This procedure is essentially just running Noether’s 2nd theorem backwards, as the original global $U(1)$ symmetry (which still exists as a special case of the local symmetry) gives rise to a conserved dynamical charge current $j^{\mu}$ which couples to $A_{\mu}$ . In other words, by creating a gauge symmetry out of thin air, one has created a new field which manifestly couples to our global $U(1)$ current.

The history behind Noether’s 2nd theorem, described for instance in [49, 50, 51], is both interesting and instructive. Right after the birth of general relativity, Albert Einstein and David Hilbert were puzzled as to the status of energy conservation in the new theory. The field equations read

$$ G^{\mu\nu}\approx 8\pi GT^{\mu\nu} $$

and the off-shell Bianchi identity implied that $\nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu\nu}=0$ . This meant that $\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}\approx 0$ had to hold automatically. At the time, this came as a surprise because Hilbert expected that energy-momentum conservation either would have to be a constraint imposed on the theory or would end up being be violated altogether. In 1915, he asked Emmy Noether, a colleague he held in high regard, to see if she could satisfactorily understand the situation.

Her resulting 1918 paper (english translation given in [52]) proved both of her theorems as well as their converses. She observed that in general relativity, the global group of translations was embedded into the diffeomorphism gauge symmetry. In section 6 of her paper, titled “A Hilbertian Assertion,” she wrote [51]:

“Given $[S]$ invariant under a group of translations, then the energy relations are improper if and only if $[S]$ is invariant under an infinite group which contains the group of translations as a subgroup.”

Read: Energy momentum conservation $\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}\approx 0$ will hold as a consequence of an off-shell identity like $\nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu\nu}=0$ if the group of translations is embedded in a larger infinite dimensional group of diffeomorphism gauge symmetries.

Let’s see for ourselves how we can derive $\nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu\nu}=0$ from diffeomorphism invariance. The Einstein Hilbert action for pure gravity is given by

$$ S=\frac{-1}{16\pi G}\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}R $$

and its variation (up to boundary terms) is

$$ \delta S=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}G^{\mu\nu}\delta g_{\mu\nu}. $$

If one then uses the variation of the metric corresponding to an infinitesimal diffeomorphism along the vector field $\xi$

$$ \delta g_{\mu\nu}=\mathcal{L}_{\xi}g_{\mu\nu}=\nabla_{\mu}\xi_{\nu}+\nabla_{\nu}\xi_{\mu} $$

under which $\delta S=0$ . Assuming $\xi_{\nu}$ is compact, we have

$$ \displaystyle 0=\delta S \displaystyle=\frac{1}{8\pi G}\int d^{4}x\,\sqrt{-g}G^{\mu\nu}\nabla_{\mu}\xi_{\nu} \displaystyle=\frac{-1}{8\pi G}\int d^{4}x\,\sqrt{-g}\nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu\nu}\xi_{\nu}. $$

Allowing $\xi_{\nu}$ to freely vary, we see that

$$ \nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu\nu}=0 $$

off-shell. Therefore, the conservation of energy momentum has the same status in gravity that the conservation of charge has in electromagnetism: they are consistency conditions required by gauge symmetry.

As a brief aside, one might wonder how an equation like $\partial_{\nu}(\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}-j^{\nu})=0$ could possibly hold off-shell when $j^{\nu}$ is not a background source but rather depends on a dynamical field, in which case we would have $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}\approx 0$ but not $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ . Take for instance the QED Lagrangian

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\rm QED}=-\frac{1}{4}F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}+\overline{\psi}(i\gamma^{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}+ieA_{\mu})-m)\psi $$

which has the gauge symmetry

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu} \displaystyle\mapsto A_{\mu}+\partial_{\mu}\lambda \displaystyle\psi \displaystyle\mapsto e^{-i\lambda}\psi. $$

The Noether current from the global $\lambda=const$ symmetry is given by

$$ j^{\mu}=e\overline{\psi}\gamma^{\mu}\psi. $$

If one computes the Noether’s-2nd-theorem off-shell identity resulting from $\mathcal{L}_{\rm QED}$ , one will find that it is just $\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=0$ . $j^{\mu}$ doesn’t appear in this equation, as it couldn’t. We can still easily derive that $j^{\mu}$ is conserved from $\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=0$ ; it just takes one extra line of algebra, namely $\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}\approx j^{\nu}$ . To sum up: Noether’s 2nd theorem can only be used to impose $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ off-shell when $j^{\mu}$ is an external current, which is very reasonable. Otherwise, it will give you $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}\approx 0$ . Interestingly, we could also derive this result by using a “half” gauge transformation where one just varies $A_{\mu}$ as $\delta A_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\lambda$ but doesn’t vary $\psi$ . As this is not a full gauge transformation which would render $\delta S=0$ off-shell, we can’t derive an off-shell equation. However, we can still evoke $\delta S\approx 0$ under this half gauge transformation to derive $\partial_{\nu}(\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}-j^{\nu})\approx 0$ .

### B.3 Noether’s 1.5th Theorem

An astute observer may notice that a one-parameter family of symmetries generated by an arbitrary infinitesimal gauge transformation can be thought of as a global symmetry. One might wonder: how does the corresponding conserved current derived from Noether’s 1st theorem behave? This question is addressed by a result we will call ‘‘Noether’s 1.5th theorem,’’ as it exists in the middle ground between her 1st and 2nd theorems.1616 16 This is a well-known fact [53] but to my knowledge had not been given a specific name in the literature. Having said that, a closely related result is called the ‘Generalized Noether Theorem’ [32].

To be specific, say that the infinitesimal gauge symmetries are parameterized by a spacetime function $f$ . The conserved current $J^{\mu}_{f}$ will satisfy $\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f}\approx 0$ . This means we can always find an anti-symmetric 2-form $K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ such that $J^{\mu}_{f}\approx\partial_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ if our spacetime has trivial de Rham cohomology. Actually, this $K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ can only be well defined up to the addition of a total derivative term of the form

$$ K_{f}^{\mu\nu}\to K_{f}^{\mu\nu}+\partial_{\rho}M^{\mu\nu\rho} $$

where $M^{\mu\nu\rho}$ is any completely anti-symmetric rank-3 tensor.

Noether’s 1.5th theorem states that there is some choice of $K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ which is locally constructed out of the fields and gauge parameter $f$ .

Note that the addition of a term $\partial_{\rho}M^{\mu\nu\rho}$ will not affect integrals of the form $\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}$ when $S$ is a closed surface. Therefore, to prove the theorem, it is sufficient to show that for any surface $S$ , the integral $\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}$ only depends on the values and derivatives of the fields and gauge parameter $f$ on the surface itself.

To examine why this “locally constructed” clause is important, let’s quickly review how $K^{\mu\nu}$ can be found in general when $\partial_{\nu}K^{\mu\nu}=J^{\mu}$ and $\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}=0$ . It can be found using the integral

$$ K^{\mu\nu}(x)=\int_{x_{0}}^{x}(J^{\mu}dx^{\nu}-J^{\nu}dx^{\mu}) $$

where we integrate along an arbitrary path connecting a basepoint $x_{0}$ to $x$ . If the path is deformed, $K^{\mu\nu}$ will change by a total derivative. To see this, one can consider a small square path in the $x^{\alpha}$ - $x^{\beta}$ plane of side length $\epsilon$ , which we can denote as “ $\square_{\alpha\beta}$ ”, and calculate that

$$ \int_{\square_{\alpha\beta}}(J^{\mu}dx^{\nu}-J^{\nu}dx^{\mu})=\epsilon^{2}\partial_{\rho}M_{\alpha\beta}^{\mu\nu\rho} $$

where

$$ M_{\alpha\beta}^{\mu\nu\rho}=-\delta^{[\mu}_{\alpha}\delta^{\nu}_{\beta}J^{\rho]}. $$

In any case, a generic $K^{\mu\nu}$ defined by such an integral will be intrinsically non-local, as its value at $x$ depends on the value $J$ at other spacetime points as well.

We will now prove Noether’s 1.5th theorem, using a modified version of the proof presented in [15]. The proof is non-constructive, meaning in practice one must just observe it holds for whatever example one is interested in.

We will crucially use the fact that $J^{\mu}_{f}$ is itself guaranteed to be locally constructed out of the fields and $f$ by its standard method of construction used in the proof of Noether’s 1st theorem. Furthermore, $J^{\mu}_{f}(x)$ will be $0$ at any spacetime points $x$ where $f(x)=0$ and its derivatives $\partial_{\mu}f(x)=0$ .

*Figure 29: $\partial V=\Sigma_{1}+\Sigma_{2}$ and $\partial\Sigma_{1}=-\partial\Sigma_{2}=S$ .*

First, choose an arbitrary 4-volume $V$ . Denote its boundary as $\partial V=\Sigma_{1}+\Sigma_{2}$ where $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ share a common boundary $\partial\Sigma_{1}=-\partial\Sigma_{2}=S$ (with a sign for orientation). A diagram is provided in Figure 29.

Notice that

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle\approx\int_{V}d^{4}x\sqrt{-g}\nabla_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f} \displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma_{1}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f}+\int_{\Sigma_{2}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f} $$

which can be rewritten as

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{1}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f}\approx-\int_{\Sigma_{2}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f}. $$

Let’s now choose an $f$ such that $f(x)=0$ when $x\in\Sigma_{2}$ and $\partial_{\mu}f(x)=0$ when $x\in S$ . The RHS of the above equation will be $0$ , proving that

$$ \int_{\Sigma_{1}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f}\approx\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{f}\approx 0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{if $f$ and its derivatives are $0$ on $S$.} $$

Because $J^{\mu}_{f}$ is derived by performing an infinitesimal gauge transformation on our fields, it is guaranteed to be linear in $f$ , meaning that

$$ \displaystyle J^{\mu}_{f_{1}}+J^{\mu}_{f_{2}} \displaystyle=J^{\mu}_{f_{1}+f_{2}} \displaystyle K^{\mu\nu}_{f_{1}}+K^{\mu\nu}_{f_{2}} \displaystyle=K^{\mu\nu}_{f_{1}+f_{2}}. $$

Therefore, we have just shown that

$$ \int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{f_{1}}\approx\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{f_{2}}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{if $f_{1}$, $f_{2}$ and their derivatives are equal on $S$.} $$

We have therefore proven that $K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ must depend locally on the gauge parameter $f$ . To complete the proof, we must also show that it depends locally on the field variables as well.

Because $K^{\mu\nu}_{f}$ depends locally on $f$ , we know that the equation

$$ \int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{f}=\int_{\Sigma_{1}}d\Sigma_{\mu}J^{\mu}_{f} $$

will still hold if on the RHS we replace $f$ with $f^{\prime}$ such that $f$ and its derivatives are equal to $f^{\prime}$ and its derivatives on $S$ . We can then take $f^{\prime}$ to be 0 outside of an arbitrarily small tubular neighborhood of $S$ . However, the RHS of the above equation would then only depend on field variables arbitrarily close to $S$ , as $J_{f^{\prime}}^{\mu}$ will be 0 wherever $f^{\prime}$ and its derivatives are $0$ . Therefore, the LHS can also only depend on field variables arbitrarily close to $S$ as well. This completes the proof of Noether’s 1.5th theorem.

A curious reader might wonder what the Noether’s-1.5th-theorem diffeomorphism 2-form is for pure GR. Given an arbitrary vector $\xi$ , it is

$$ K_{\xi}^{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{16\pi G}(\nabla^{\mu}\xi^{\nu}-\nabla^{\nu}\xi^{\mu}). $$

Note that the $J^{\mu}_{\xi}\approx\nabla_{\nu}K_{\xi}^{\mu\nu}=0$ if $\xi$ is a Killing vector of a particular solution $g_{\mu\nu}$ . This is because such a transformation represents an “empty” transformation $\delta g_{\mu\nu}=\mathcal{L}_{\xi}g_{\mu\nu}=0$ on that solution, meaning the Noether current must vanish.1717 17 This is the same thing that happens in EM when $\lambda=1$ and we recover Gauss’s law. This means that the surface of integration of $K^{\mu\nu}_{\xi}$ can be deformed freely without changing the value of the integral. This is a very powerful observation when coupled with the fact that $K^{\mu\nu}_{\xi}$ depends locally on $\xi$ and the metric. For instance, if one has an arbitrary spacetime which asymptotically approaches some fixed background metric $\overline{g}_{\mu\nu}$ at large distances, one can use a Killing vector $\xi$ of $\overline{g}_{\mu\nu}$ to define surface charges $Q_{\xi}=\int_{S}dS_{\mu\nu}K^{\mu\nu}_{\xi}$ where $S$ is topologically a large 2-sphere at infinity. $Q_{\xi}$ will not change if $S$ is deformed as long as $S$ remains sufficiently far away from the interior of the spacetime where $g_{\mu\nu}$ can deviate from $\overline{g}_{\mu\nu}$ and $\xi$ will no longer satisfy Killing’s equation. These surface charges will give, for instance, the Komar mass and Komar angular momentum when one takes $\xi=\partial_{t}$ or $\partial_{\phi}$ for asymptotically Kerr spacetimes.

Actually, some of these Komar charges will be off by relative factors of 2. These discrepancies will be resolved if one considers more intricate constructions of diffeomorphism surface charges using the covariant phase space formalism. This was done, for instance, in Wald’s classic paper [30] where he gave a Noetherian proof of the first law of black hole thermodynamics. However, the most general “best” proscription for defining these surface charges is still a matter of debate, with different approaches used by different practitioners in different contexts [32, 54, 55, 56, 57].

## Appendix C Results From Classical Electromagnetism

### C.1 Green’s functions

Say you have a massless scalar field satisfying the inhomogeneous wave equation

$$ \partial^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\phi=j(x) $$

where $j(x)$ is an external source. We are interested in solving for $\phi$ (given some boundary conditions) for any $j(x)$ . To do this let’s find the Green’s function $G(x)$ which satisfies

$$ \partial^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}G(x)=\delta^{4}(x). $$

We can use the Fourier transforms

$$ \displaystyle G(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d^{4}k\;e^{-ikx}\widetilde{G}(k) \displaystyle\delta^{4}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d^{4}k\;e^{-ikx} $$

to rewrite (C.2) as

$$ -k^{2}\widetilde{G}(k)=1. $$

Now, the above equation does not specify a unique solution for $\widetilde{G}(k)$ due to the fact that one cannot divide by $k^{2}$ when it is 0. This non-uniqueness was actually inevitable. Note that if you have a function $F$ that satisfies the homogeneous wave equation $\partial^{2}F=0$ , then $G+F$ will still solve (C.2). So the non-invertibility of $\partial^{2}$ is due to the fact that there are many possible solutions which differ by solutions to the homogeneous equation. In particular, these different solutions will all have different boundary conditions.

Two possible Green’s functions are the “retarded” and “advanced” solutions

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{G}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rm ret\\
\rm adv\end{subarray}}(k) \displaystyle=\frac{-1}{(k_{0}\pm i\epsilon)^{2}-\vec{k}^{2}} \displaystyle G_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rm ret\\
\rm adv\end{subarray}}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{-1}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d^{4}k\frac{e^{-ikx}}{(k_{0}\pm i\epsilon)^{2}-\vec{k}^{2}}. $$

Note that the integrands have two poles in the complex $k_{0}$ plane.

*Figure 30: Pole locations for retarded and advanced Green’s functions.*

Let’s evaluate, say, $G_{\rm ret}(x)$ . Note that in the numerator of (C.7) we have $e^{-ik_{0}x_{0}}$ . If $x_{0}<0$ , this dampens for $\imaginary(k_{0})>0$ and explodes for $\imaginary(k_{0})<0$ . If $x_{0}>0$ , this dampens for $\imaginary(k_{0})<0$ and explodes for $\imaginary(k_{0})>0$ .

Consider a large semi-circular contour like $\cap$ or $\cup$ . Because the overall power of the $\widetilde{G}$ integral is roughly $\int\tfrac{dk_{0}}{k_{0}^{2}}\sim 1/k_{0}$ , this will go to zero for large radius as long as the exponential factor $e^{-ik_{0}x_{0}}$ doesn’t explode. So for $x_{0}<0$ the upper semi circular integral is 0, while for $x_{0}>0$ the lower semi circular integral is 0.

*Figure 31: These large semi circles in green integrate to 0 for $\widetilde{G}_{\rm ret}$ .*

Now, our actual contour of interest is $k_{0}$ going from $-\infty$ to $\infty$ . In the case of $x_{0}<0$ when we close the contour we don’t enclose the poles, and therefore the integral is 0. However, when $x_{0}>0$ we do pick up the poles and get a non-zero result.

In order to easily find the residues of the integrand, one can use the difference of squares

$$ \frac{1}{(k_{0}+i\epsilon)^{2}-\vec{k}^{2}}=\frac{1}{(k_{0}+|\vec{k}|+i\epsilon)(k_{0}-|\vec{k}|+i\epsilon)}. $$

After using the residue theorem, (rembering to multiply by $-1$ due to the clockwise contour) we get

$$ \displaystyle G_{\rm ret}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d^{3}k\frac{2\pi i}{2|\vec{k}|}e^{i\vec{k}\vec{x}}(e^{-i|\vec{k}|x_{0}}-e^{i|\vec{k}|x_{0}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{3}k\frac{1}{|\vec{k}|}e^{i\vec{k}\vec{x}}\sin( |\bk| x_0) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int\kappa^{2}d\kappa\sin\theta d\theta\;\frac{1}{\kappa}e^{i\kappa|\vec{x}|\cos\theta}\sin( \kappa x_0) $$

where in the last line, $\kappa=|\vec{k}|$ and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{k}$ and $\vec{x}$ . Substituting $u=\cos\theta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle G_{\rm ret}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\kappa^{2}d\kappa\int_{-1}^{+1}du\;\frac{1}{\kappa}e^{i\kappa|\vec{x}|u}\sin( \kappa x_0) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{2}|\vec{x}|}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\kappa\;2\sin(\kappa|\bx|)\sin(\kappa x_0) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{2}|\vec{x}|}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\kappa\;\sin(\kappa|\bx|)\sin(\kappa x_0) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{2}|\vec{x}|}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}d\kappa\;\frac{1}{2}(e^{i\kappa(x_{0}-|\vec{x}|)}-e^{i\kappa(x_{0}+|\vec{x}|)}) $$

where for the last equality you must you use the $\sin/\cos$ addition formulas and that the integral of an odd function is 0. Note that the results are just delta functions, with the second one is always being 0 because $x_{0}$ and $|\vec{x}|$ are both positive. Therefore

$$ \displaystyle G_{\rm ret}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{4\pi|\vec{x}|}\delta(x_{0}-|\vec{x}|) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{2\pi}\delta(x^{2}). $$

Note that from the definition of the $G_{\rm ret}$ and $G_{\rm adv}$ in (C.7), we manifestly have

$$ G_{\rm adv}(x)=G_{\rm ret}(-x). $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle G_{\rm adv}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{\Theta(-x_{0})}{2\pi}\delta(x^{2}). $$

We can now clearly see what the boundary conditions of $G_{\rm ret}$ and $G_{\rm adv}$ are. $G_{\rm ret}$ vanishes for $x_{0}<0$ and $G_{\rm adv}$ vanishes for $x_{0}>0$ .

There is another useful way to write $G_{\rm ret}$ . Using (C.9), we see

$$ \displaystyle G_{\rm ret}(x) \displaystyle=i\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{3}k\frac{1}{2|\vec{k}|}e^{i\vec{k}\vec{x}}(e^{-i|\vec{k}|x_{0}}-e^{i|\vec{k}|x_{0}}) \displaystyle=i\frac{\Theta(x_{0})}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}k\;\mathrm{sign}(k_{0})e^{-ikx}\delta(k^{2}). $$

To complete the discussion, let’s define the difference of the two Green’s functions

$$ G_{(-)}(x)\equiv G_{\rm ret}(x)-G_{\rm adv}(x). $$

Using (C.18), along with (C.21), we find

$$ \displaystyle G_{(-)}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}k\;\mathrm{sign}(k_{0})e^{-ikx}\delta(k^{2}). $$

From (C.23) we can see that $G_{(-)}(x)$ manifestly solves the homogeneous wave equation $\partial^{2}G_{(-)}=0$ . This had to be the case because it was defined as the difference between $G_{\rm ret}$ and $G_{\rm adv}$ which each solve the inhomogeneous equation.

### C.2 EM radiation

The following is mostly taken from section 1.3.2 of [29]. If we have the gauge field $A_{\mu}$ and field strength tensor

$$ F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu} $$

Maxwell’s laws are

$$ \partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=j^{\nu}. $$

If we use Lorenz gauge

$$ \partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}=0 $$

then

$$ \partial_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}(\partial^{\mu}A^{\nu}-\partial^{\nu}A^{\mu})=\partial_{\mu}\partial^{\mu}A^{\nu} $$

and Maxwell’s laws become

$$ \partial_{\mu}\partial^{\mu}A^{\nu}=j^{\nu} $$

which is just four copies of the scalar wave equation (C.1).

We can immediately write the gauge field in the presence of the source.1818 18 One might question why we exclusively use the retarded propagator, as this seems to break time reversal symmetry. The answer is simply that the advanced propagator corresponds to a non-physical situation where a perfectly arranged sphere of light (which has existed since the beginning of the time) has been converging on our charge only to get perfectly “sucked up” by it just as the charge accelerates. These initial conditions require an absurd degree of fine-tuning and morally violate the second law of thermodynamics [58].

$$ \displaystyle A^{\mu}(x) \displaystyle=\int d^{4}yG_{\rm ret}(x-y)j^{\mu}(y). $$

However, going forward, we’re actually going to use a different expression. Let us substitute in

$$ G_{\rm ret}=G_{(-)}+G_{\rm adv}. $$

Note that $G_{\rm adv}$ only has support in the past lightcone and thus can’t account for any radiated light. Therefore, assuming we are only concerned with radiation emitted towards the future, we can write

$$ A^{\mu}_{\rm rad}(x)=\int d^{4}yG_{(-)}(x-y)j^{\mu}(y). $$

Because $G_{(-)}$ solves free $(j^{\mu}=0)$ equations of motion, it is just a sum of plane waves, which means it should be thought of as describing free moving light waves. It is sometimes called $G_{\rm rad}$ for this reason.

Next, we write the current $j^{\mu}(x)$ in terms of its Fourier components

$$ j^{\mu}(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d^{4}k\;e^{-ikx}\tilde{j}^{\mu}(k). $$

Note the reality condition

$$ \tilde{j}_{\mu}(k)=\tilde{j}_{\mu}^{*}(-k). $$

We rewrite (C.31) using (C.23) as

$$ A^{\mu}_{\rm rad}(x)=\frac{i}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}k\;\mathrm{sign}(k_{0})e^{-ikx}\delta(k^{2})\tilde{j}^{\mu}(k). $$

We now have an expression for the total radiated field, but one might wonder how much of the field is radiated in each mode. Recall that in Lorenz gauge, light waves take the form

$$ A_{\mu}(x)\propto\varepsilon_{\mu}e^{-ikx} $$

where $k^{2}=0$ . Here, $\varepsilon_{\mu}$ is called a ‘polarization vector.’ Lorenz gauge implies the following condition:

$$ \partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}=0\hskip 21.33955pt\implies\hskip 21.33955ptk_{\mu}\varepsilon^{\mu}=0. $$

Furthermore, the residual gauge symmetry of

$$ A_{\mu}\sim A_{\mu}+\partial_{\mu}\lambda\hskip 14.22636pt\text{where}\hskip 14.22636pt\partial_{\mu}\partial^{\mu}\lambda=0 $$

implies the following redundancy of

$$ \varepsilon_{\mu}\sim\varepsilon_{\mu}+\widetilde{\lambda}k_{\mu} $$

for any number $\widetilde{\lambda}$ . This leaves two linearly independent spacelike polarization vectors, which we call $\varepsilon_{\mu}^{a}$ for $a=1,2$ . In a Fourier decomposition, these depend on $k$ as $\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}=\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}(k)$ but we will suppress this dependence in our notation. We can choose them to satisfy

$$ (\varepsilon^{a})^{2}=-1\hskip 28.45274pt\varepsilon^{1}_{\mu}\varepsilon^{2\mu}=0\hskip 28.45274pt(\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu})^{*}=\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu} $$

for each $k$ . This means we have the following “identity” operator (up to gauge transformation) which we can act on $A^{\mu}_{\rm rad}$ in (C.34). It can be written as

$$ \delta^{\mu}_{\nu}=-\sum_{a=1,2}\varepsilon^{a\mu}\varepsilon^{a}_{\nu}+\mathrm{gauge}. $$

This also means that we have the two projection operators

$$ (P^{a})_{\;\;\nu}^{\mu}=-\varepsilon^{a\mu}\varepsilon^{a}_{\nu}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{(no $a$ sum)} $$

which can use to project a wave onto its polarization components.

Next we write the field strength tensor as

$$ \displaystyle F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm rad}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int d^{4}k\;e^{-ikx}\mathrm{sign}(k_{0})\delta(k^{2})\big(k^{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\nu}-k^{\nu}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\big) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}e^{i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{x}}(k^{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\nu}-k^{\nu}\tilde{j}^{\mu}) $$

where we used the formula

$$ \int d^{4}k\delta(k^{2})=\int\frac{d^{3}k}{2|\vec{k}|}\sum_{k_{0}=\pm|\vec{k}|} $$

and simply chose not to write the sum over $k_{0}=\pm|\vec{k}|$ because it’s notationally cumbersome and commonly suppressed.

The energy density of the field is given by the stress energy tensor as

$$ T^{0}_{\;\;0}=-F^{\mu 0}F_{\mu 0}+\tfrac{1}{4}\delta^{0}_{0}F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}. $$

Let’s now find the total energy of the field $F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm rad}$ in (C.43). First we evaluate $\int d^{3}xF^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\int d^{3}xF^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{6}}\int d^{3}x\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{2k_{0}^{\prime}}e^{i\vec{x}\cdot(\vec{k}+\vec{k}^{\prime})}2(k^{\mu}k^{\prime}_{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\nu}\tilde{j}^{\prime}_{\nu}-k^{\mu}\tilde{j}_{\mu}{k^{\prime}}^{\nu}\tilde{j}_{\nu}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{-4k_{0}^{2}}(-2)(k^{2}\tilde{j}^{\nu}\tilde{j}_{\nu}^{*}-k^{\mu}\tilde{j}_{\mu}k^{\mu}\tilde{j}_{\mu}^{*}) \displaystyle=0. $$

The whole expression is zero because (i) $k^{2}=0$ in the integral and (ii) $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ implies $k^{\mu}\tilde{j}_{\mu}(k)=0$ . Next, let’s evaluate $\int d^{3}xF^{\mu 0}F_{\mu 0}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\int d^{3}xF^{\mu 0}F_{\mu 0} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{6}}\int d^{3}x\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}\frac{d^{3}k^{\prime}}{2k_{0}^{\prime}}e^{i\vec{x}\cdot(\vec{k}+\vec{k}^{\prime})}(k^{\mu}\tilde{j}^{0}-k^{0}\tilde{j}^{\mu})(k_{\mu}^{\prime}\tilde{j}_{0}^{\prime}-k_{0}^{\prime}\tilde{j}_{\mu}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int\frac{d^{3}k}{-4k_{0}^{2}}(-1)(k_{0}^{2}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\tilde{j}_{\mu}^{*}) \displaystyle=\frac{-1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{k_{0}>0}\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}k_{0}\sum_{a=1,2}\left|\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\right|^{2}. $$

To get the last line, we acted with the decomposition of the identity operator (C.40) on $A_{\mathrm{rad}}^{\mu}$ in (C.34), which essentially allows us to replace $\tilde{j}^{\mu}\mapsto-\sum_{a}\varepsilon^{a\mu}\varepsilon^{a}_{\;\nu}\tilde{j}^{\nu}$ .

Therefore, the total energy of radiated photons is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E} \displaystyle=\int d^{3}T^{0}_{\;0} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{k_{0}>0}\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}k_{0}\sum_{a=1,2}\left|\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\right|^{2}. $$

The amount of energy emitted per momentum vector $k^{\mu}$ and polarization $\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}$ is

$$ d\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}k_{0}\left|\varepsilon^{a}_{\mu}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\right|^{2}. $$

We can write the polarization summed version as

$$ d\mathcal{E}=\frac{-1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{d^{3}k}{2k_{0}}k_{0}\tilde{j}^{\mu}\tilde{j}^{*}_{\mu}. $$

### C.3 The Liénard–Wiechert potential

If we have a single point particle of charge $e$ tracing out a path in spacetime $x(\tau)$ ,

$$ j^{\mu}(x)=e\int d\tau\;\frac{dx^{\mu}(\tau)}{d\tau}\delta^{4}[x-x(\tau)]. $$

Let us quickly check that $\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=0$ . Note that the 1D delta function satisfies

$$ \partial_{\tau}\delta\left[x-f(\tau)\right]=-\frac{df}{d\tau}\partial_{x}\delta\left[x-f(\tau)\right] $$

so

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}(x) \displaystyle=e\int d\tau\;\frac{dx^{\mu}(\tau)}{d\tau}\frac{-1}{dx^{\mu}/d\tau}\partial_{\tau}\delta^{4}\left[x-x(\tau)\right] \displaystyle=e\int d\tau(-4)\partial_{\tau}\delta^{4}\left[x-x(\tau)\right] \displaystyle=0 $$

where in the last line we integrated by parts.

In Lorenz gauge, $A^{\mu}(x)$ is given by (C.29)

$$ \displaystyle A^{\mu}(x) \displaystyle=\int d^{4}y\,G_{\rm ret}(x-y)j^{\mu}(y) \displaystyle=e\int d\tau\frac{dx^{\mu}}{d\tau}G_{\rm ret}(x-x(\tau)) \displaystyle=\frac{e}{2\pi}\int d\tau\frac{dx^{\mu}}{d\tau}\Theta(x^{0}-x^{0}(\tau))\delta[(x-x(\tau))^{2}]. $$

At this point we must use the delta function identity

$$ \delta(f(\tau))=\frac{\delta(\tau-\tau_{*})}{|f^{\prime}(\tau_{*})|} $$

where $\tau_{*}$ is defined by $f(\tau_{*})=0$ . The derivative of $(x-x(\tau))^{2}$ is

$$ \frac{d}{d\tau}(x-x(\tau))^{2}=-2\dot{x}\cdot(x-x(\tau)). $$

The above quantity is guaranteed to be negative because $\dot{x}^{\mu}$ is forward-pointing and timelike while $(x-x(\tau))^{\mu}$ is forward-pointing and null. Therefore, the absolute value introduces a minus sign and

$$ A^{\mu}(x)=\frac{e}{4\pi}\frac{\dot{x}_{\rm ret}^{\mu}}{\dot{x}_{\rm ret}\cdot(x-x_{\rm ret})} $$

where $x^{\mu}_{\rm ret}$ is the unique point on the path $x^{\mu}(\tau)$ that satisfies

$$ \displaystyle x^{0}_{\rm ret}< \displaystyle x^{0} \displaystyle(x-x_{\rm ret})^{2} \displaystyle=0. $$

Let’s now find the expression for the potential created by a particle which moves at a constant velocity $\vec{\beta}$ and passes through the origin. This implies $x_{\rm ret}=(t_{\rm ret},\vec{\beta}t_{\rm ret})$ . To evaluate $A^{\mu}(t,\vec{r})$ , we must first solve for $t_{\rm ret}$ using the equation

$$ \displaystyle t-t_{\rm ret} \displaystyle=|\vec{r}-\vec{\beta}t_{\rm ret}| \displaystyle t^{2}-2tt_{\rm ret}+t_{\rm ret}^{2} \displaystyle=r^{2}-2\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta}t_{\rm ret}+\beta^{2}t_{\rm ret}^{2} $$

*Figure 32: Say a charged particle moves along the line parameterized by $(t,\vec{\beta}t)$ . If an observer is located at a point $(t,\vec{r})$ , then $(t_{\rm ret},\vec{\beta}t_{\rm ret})$ is defined to be the point on its past lightcone that intersects the particle’s path.*

We can solve this using the quadratic equation and taking the smaller root because we want the point in the past light cone.

$$ (1-\beta^{2})t_{\rm ret}^{2}-2(t-\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta})t_{\rm ret}+(t^{2}-r^{2})=0 $$

$$ t_{\rm ret}=\frac{t-\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta}-\sqrt{(t-\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta})-(1-\beta^{2})(t^{2}-r^{2})}}{1-\beta^{2}} $$

Next, note that

$$ \displaystyle(1,\vec{\beta})\cdot(t-t_{\rm ret},\vec{r}-\vec{\beta}t_{\rm ret}) \displaystyle=t-\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta}-(1-\beta^{2})t_{\rm ret} \displaystyle=\sqrt{(t-\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta})-(1-\beta^{2})(t^{2}-r^{2})} \displaystyle=\sqrt{(\vec{r}-\vec{\beta}t)^{2}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta})^{2}-\beta^{2}r^{2}} $$

so

$$ A^{\mu}(t,\vec{r})=\frac{e}{4\pi}\frac{(1,\vec{\beta})}{\sqrt{(\vec{r}-\vec{\beta}t)^{2}+(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{\beta})^{2}-\beta^{2}r^{2}}}. $$
